                <article class="article">
                    
                    
                        
                        
                        
                            
                            <div class="hlFld-Fulltext"><div id="embedded-pdf-target" class="with-border"></div><div class="pb-dropzone" data-pb-dropzone="contentNavigationDropZoneAbs"><div class="widget gql-content-navigation none  widget-none" id="2ffb43c7-15dc-4c79-9e29-8e4bed9b3d1e">
        
        

        <div class="wrapped ">
            
            <div class="widget-body body body-none "><div class="ajaxWidget" data-ajax-widget="gql-content-navigation" data-ajax-widget-id="2ffb43c7-15dc-4c79-9e29-8e4bed9b3d1e" data-ajax-observe="true">
    
</div></div>
        </div>
    </div></div><div class="NLM_sec NLM_sec_level_1" id="S0001"><p class="first"><img src="/cms/asset/13851123-f18d-4dc8-860b-7adc57fe9474/rrob_a_2567376_ilg0001_c.jpg" loading="lazy" height="975" width="650"></p><p>As they prepared this volume in 2022, the coeditors could not have fathomed what would transpire in higher education in the United States in 2025: the relentless attacks on academic freedom and institutional independence; the systematic defunding, and thus the dismantling, of the well-respected U.S. research enterprise; and the weaponization of diversity, equity, inclusion, and justice (DEIJ) rhetorics among other things. Although elite higher educational institutions in the United States have borne the brunt of the Trump administration’s attacks thus far, they reflect larger patterns of rising nationalisms across the globe that are attempting to tamp down free thought and the independence of educational institutions. Against this global political landscape, voices that bravely continue to advocate for DEIJ, like the ones proffered in this book, are all the more needed to combat the climate of intimidation and vulnerability. As this book is written by and for geographers, it serves as an imp­ortant reminder that geography, as a discipline, has a responsibility and ethical imperative to use the scope of its resources—disciplinary knowledge, research tools, technological adva­ncement and institutional and fin­a­ncial resources—to serve the needs of all of its members and protect those who are most marginal and at risk of being silenced. Geography and geographers must respond to global political threats in a timely, ethical manner.</p><p>Of course, many subdisciplines in geography emerged precisely to address these concerns head on. Feminist, labor and postcolonial geographies, critical urban studies, and critical geographic information systems (GIS) have long ­produced impactful histories of inter­disci­pli­nary scholarship that have attended to questions of social inequality, power, and transformative change. Yet, decades of cutting-edge theorizing of race, gender, and other social differences have barely made a dent in improving the racial composition of the discipline. In one of the book’s early chapters, Jordan and Raji point out that although gender representation has steadily increased in the discipline over the past couple of decades, undergraduates and graduate geography and geoscience programs are more than 80 percent white in the United States and the United Kingdom with very little change from previous decades. Furthermore, early career researchers of color in these fields face disproportionately lower levels of funding than white researchers. Troublingly, as I also learned through reading the book, Black and Latinx specialty groups have only been established a decade or so ago despite calls throughout the 1990s and early 2000s that highlighted this need (K. Davis, Nimoh, and Reason; Ybarra and Munoz). It raises the question as to why geography is slow to apply the discipline’s radical thinking to the discipline itself.</p><p>Coeditors Chen and Eaves write that “our goal [is] to create a growing community of theories and praxis for all interested in understanding, fostering, advancing, imagining, and envisioning a more diverse, equitable, inclusive, and just intellectual community of geography, including a space from which all under-represented geographers can speak” (p. 3). This book is an excellent starting place to learn about previous and ongoing DEIJ work in the discipline and unique projects building on these efforts. A strength of the book is the quality and range of the chapter contributions, and each chapter takes on a salient issue many geographers confront in their work, be it in their teaching, research, policy development, or efforts to promote institutional change, and explores a specific DEIJ-related issue within it. The focus spans the Anglo-American world with contributors from a range of backgrounds and identities hailing from the United Kingdom, North America, Southeast Asia, and the South Pacific. The chapter contributors probe the issues with thoughtfulness and depth, uncovering multilayered dimensions to the problems, and put forth novel ways of addressing them. Many of the contributors also thoughtfully acknowledge their own positionalities and locate themselves on a global spectrum to identify the intersecting layers of social privilege or marginality that shape their perspectives—an intentional effort to put DEIJ principles into practice. I walked away from reading this volume invigorated with fresh new ideas, tools, and additional resources to deepen both my DEIJ thinking and praxis as a geographer.</p><p>The book is organized into three parts (or as a sequence of inquiries as the coeditors also put it): “Understanding DEI and Justice in Geography” (“what do we know?”); “Praxis and Examples of Fostering DEI and Justice in Geography” (“what can we do?”), and “Future of DEI and Justice in Geography: New Tools, Methods and Directions” (“what is next?”). Following the introduction, Chief Strategy Officer for the American Association of Geographers (AAG) Risha RaQuelle provides a framework for understanding institutional change and the ways the AAG has been advancing DEIJ goals since the murder of George Floyd, representing efforts to directly cultivate DEIJ at the disciplinary level in the United States. The subsequent first part “sets the epistemic and empirical foundations for DEI and justice in geography” (p. 5), and is the largest of the three subsequent parts. It consists of nine chapters, making up almost half the book. Most of the chapters that survey and locate the conversation in the discipline on a single axis of social grouping: Black, Latinx, Indigenous, Asian American, international, (dis-)abled and queer geographies, with the aforementioned chapter on the racial composition of geography and geoscience students in the United States and United Kingdom framing the part.</p><p>My reaction to the chapter-by-chapter sequencing is a bit mixed: On the one hand, each chapter gets readers up to speed about the work being done in each of these subfields. Collectively, they make the important point about shifting the foci of DEIJ conversations from issues of representation, belonging, and procedural justice to ones of epistemology, knowledge creation, and analytic frameworks and methodologies, what Mei-Singh, Cheng, and Chen, borrowing from Shih (<span class="ref-lnk lazy-ref bibr"><a data-rid="CIT0011" href="#" data-behaviour="toggle-ref" data-ref-type="bibr" data-label="reference" data-registered=""><span class="off-screen">Citation</span>2016</a></span>), refer to as “epistemic justice.” The chapters also highlight the challenges, as Anindita Datta puts it, of the intense emotional labor of “negotiating race, gender, and location in white field.” Much of this work addresses what Settles and colleagues (Settles et al. <span class="ref-lnk lazy-ref bibr"><a data-rid="CIT0009" href="#" data-behaviour="toggle-ref" data-ref-type="bibr" data-label="reference" data-registered=""><span class="off-screen">Citation</span>2021</a></span>; Settles et al. <span class="ref-lnk lazy-ref bibr"><a data-rid="CIT0010" href="#" data-behaviour="toggle-ref" data-ref-type="bibr" data-label="reference" data-registered=""><span class="off-screen">Citation</span>2022</a></span>) referred to as “epistemic exclusion”—the way unconscious bias operates through the gatekeeping mechanisms of the academy. Epistemic justice aims to rectify the emotional exhaustion of epistemic exclusion by broadening the scope of epistemology and methodological tools to affirm cultural- or community-based ways of knowing. It is brilliantly illustrated in the chapter by Megan Ybarra and Lorena Munoz when they discuss their efforts to create a Latinx geographies specialty group (instead of an affinity group) within the AAG.</p><p>At the same time, put together in this way, the chapters felt a bit schematic and not fully reflective of the complex, intersectional ways these categories play out in the real world. I caution against presenting social groups as neatly bounded categories because of the way they can be easily taken for granted by those less well-versed in DEIJ thought. The concepts of intersectionality, positionalities, and ambiguous identities are illustrated in individual chapters in this part and in subsequent chapters in the book, most poignantly in the chapter by Fitzgerald, Garrett, and Sharma. Given the part’s length and centrality to the book, however, it would have been helpful if the coeditors discussed these concepts in more explicit terms to frame this part, perhaps through an introductory or concluding part that clarified the intersectional, overlapping nature of social identity categories. They do offer a bit of this analysis in the introduction, but it could be deepened and emphasized in the first part to ensure that the messiness and fluidity of these categories get reinforced there.</p><p>Similarly, the part could benefit from an additional chapter on critical whiteness in geography. Focusing solely on marginalized or underrepresented groups makes it easy to assume that DEIJ advocacy is the responsibility of those most negatively affected by mainstream policies and practices—a conclusion easily drawn without examples that analyze white privilege. There are several chapters by geographers who identify as white and critically address the persistent whiteness in the discipline (e.g., through decolonial school geography in the United Kingdom, teaching geography courses from a social justice perspective at predominantly white institutions as a white instructor in the United States). An explicit chapter on critical whiteness in the epistemologically focused “what do we know?” part, however, might clarify how geography, as a discipline with roots in Western colonialism, resource extractivism, and imperialism, has been used to justify racial hierarchies and conquest of non-Western lands and cultures (Agnew and Duncan <span class="ref-lnk lazy-ref bibr"><a data-rid="CIT0002" href="#" data-behaviour="toggle-ref" data-ref-type="bibr" data-label="reference" data-registered=""><span class="off-screen">Citation</span>2011</a></span>). It has also been used in more contemporary racialized and racist land-use and spatial planning projects like redlining and urban decline (Aalbers <span class="ref-lnk lazy-ref bibr"><a data-rid="CIT0001" href="#" data-behaviour="toggle-ref" data-ref-type="bibr" data-label="reference" data-registered=""><span class="off-screen">Citation</span>2014</a></span>), the exploitation of “uninhabited” Native American lands (Sands <span class="ref-lnk lazy-ref bibr"><a data-rid="CIT0008" href="#" data-behaviour="toggle-ref" data-ref-type="bibr" data-label="reference" data-registered=""><span class="off-screen">Citation</span>2011</a></span>), and the justification of South African townships (Robinson <span class="ref-lnk lazy-ref bibr"><a data-rid="CIT0007" href="#" data-behaviour="toggle-ref" data-ref-type="bibr" data-label="reference" data-registered=""><span class="off-screen">Citation</span>1997</a></span>). Coming to terms with geography’s complicity in the creation of systemic inequalities and social injustice means challenging the Eurocentric legacies underpinning much of mainstream geographical knowledge and practices. In drawing out these arguments, such a chapter could illustrate the ways that knowledge is not objective, neutral, and value-free; it is inherently racialized in the same ways whiteness is also racialized. This explanation could amplify the arguments made by the other contributors that highlight how culturally rooted, racialized epistemologies advance disciplinary knowledge in important—and historically overlooked—ways.</p><p>The subsequent two parts, which make up another ten chapters and the second half of the book, cover specific ways in which DEIJ is being practiced in geography and give examples of tools that can be used to continue building on this work. A wide range of important topics are represented here, topics that need to be—but are rarely—addressed in ongoing professional development for geographers. In Part II (“what can we do?”), examples include decolonial and inclusive teaching methods as previously mentioned (Puttick and Cope), institutionalizing DEIJ policies and practices at the unit level (Skop and Li), and developing guidelines for safe, inclusive, and community-engaged field work (Alwan et al.). Part III (“what is next?”) highlights a range of novel geographic tools and methodologies, like using GIS to map health inequalities (Jung); integrating (virtual) field work into teaching (York, Hurrell, and Hutchinson); and using games, podcasting, and crafting as tools for radical storytelling (H. A. Davis and Alderman), among others. The contributions in this part are grounded in praxis and real-world examples, so they address some of the messy, overlapping complexities I was seeking in the first part. At the same time, the authors helpfully discuss ways their projects could be adapted for other contexts and settings. Given how different each project is from one another, each part would benefit if the coeditors synthesized the chapters to explicitly identify key takeaways, general principles, or strategies “to practice DEIJ in geography,” instead of leaving it to readers to deduce.</p><p>One observation about the book as a whole is that it leans heavily toward the academic. Most (but not all) of the contributors have academic credentials and affiliations, and the approaches and topics might appeal most to academic geographers. Let me make two points about this: First, for a book that is academic in orientation, I might suggest discussing the ever-increasing corporatization of academic labor and the impacts of the resulting growing toxicity of academia as a profession on scholars from underrepresented backgrounds. There is a great deal of literature on this topic outside of geography (S. M. Davis <span class="ref-lnk lazy-ref bibr"><a data-rid="CIT0003" href="#" data-behaviour="toggle-ref" data-ref-type="bibr" data-label="reference" data-registered=""><span class="off-screen">Citation</span>2024</a></span>; Pittman <span class="ref-lnk lazy-ref bibr"><a data-rid="CIT0006" href="#" data-behaviour="toggle-ref" data-ref-type="bibr" data-label="reference" data-registered=""><span class="off-screen">Citation</span>2025</a></span>; Niemann, Gutiérrez y Muhs, and González <span class="ref-lnk lazy-ref bibr"><a data-rid="CIT0005" href="#" data-behaviour="toggle-ref" data-ref-type="bibr" data-label="reference" data-registered=""><span class="off-screen">Citation</span>2020</a></span>) and individual chapters in the first part do take some of this up (e.g., Fabris). Much of this literature discusses the isolation and “cultural tax” of being the sole faculty member from an underrepresented group in one’s department or discipline and the increasingly extractive, dehumanizing nature of having one’s scholarship and teaching measured by productivity metrics while working within increasingly bureaucratized institutions led by a disproportionate number of highly paid leaders from the managerial class (Slaughter and Rhoades <span class="ref-lnk lazy-ref bibr"><a data-rid="CIT0012" href="#" data-behaviour="toggle-ref" data-ref-type="bibr" data-label="reference" data-registered=""><span class="off-screen">Citation</span>2004</a></span>; Washburn <span class="ref-lnk lazy-ref bibr"><a data-rid="CIT0013" href="#" data-behaviour="toggle-ref" data-ref-type="bibr" data-label="reference" data-registered=""><span class="off-screen">Citation</span>2008</a></span>). The demographic cliff, institutional fiscal crises, rising student debt, and the global pandemic have only exacerbated these issues, all of which took place before the second election of Trump. In response, departments and disciplines are downsizing and merging, and institutions are shuttering in their entirety, creating an even greater scarcity of sustainable career options on the academic job market. As geographers from underrepresented groups, how do we navigate or even make sense of this terrain? How do we reestablish a sense of self and agency over our labor and find authentic support for our work? Is a career in academic geography even worth it? In a profession with a future that is so unpredictable, how do we advise graduate and undergraduate students, especially from similarly underrepresented backgrounds, who might want to emulate our career choices? It is heartbreaking to consider, but given factors affecting the profession overall, is it possible that steering students away from academia is a means to foster DEIJ in geography? There is a lot of room to discuss the ways scholars from underrepresented backgrounds in our discipline negotiate or push back against academia’s unrelenting demands.</p><p>Second, we need to broaden the conversation to include geographers outside of academic geography. Those adjacent to or outside of academic geography deserve to be served by these conversations as well. From my own experiences on the margins of academia (as a non-tenure-track lecturer), many nonacademic geographers do not feel they have a place in mainstream professional geography associations because of the perceived requirement that members focus heavily on research. Nonacademic geographers confront very different sets of DEIJ issues in their workplaces—issues that academics could possibly learn from, but that they, and the professional organizations that serve them, do not take up as often. If we are going to take inclusion seriously, we need to bring in voices and experiences outside the academic realm and similarly expand support by our professional associations. What does DEIJ look like for someone who teaches AP Human Geography at an urban high school? Or for a federal worker who is no longer permitted to use the language of “diversity, equity and inclusion” in their workplace? Or for someone who is head of a food justice nonprofit or an entrepreneur running her own GIS consulting firm? Incorporating these perspectives can showcase the diverse range of professions in which geographers work while bringing in different sets of questions, concerns and analytical lenses to DEIJ in geography. In turn, it also broadens what DEIJ in geography looks like and who is served by this profession.</p><p class="last">Overall<i>, How to Foster Diversity, Equity, Inclusion, and Justice in Geography</i> is an excellent starting place for learning and garnering ideas about how to put these values into practice in our field. It helped me think more deeply about how we can widen the scope of inclusion and justice in our field, some suggestions about which I have offered here. Clearly, in the current political climate, expanding knowledge and praxis under the banner of DEIJ will be harder to achieve. Although we might change the name, the framing, or the approach of what we do, it is important that, unlike the corporations and institutions who preemptively shed their commitments to DEIJ in the wake of Trump’s second election (Naidu and Jessop <span class="ref-lnk lazy-ref bibr"><a data-rid="CIT0004" href="#" data-behaviour="toggle-ref" data-ref-type="bibr" data-label="reference" data-registered=""><span class="off-screen">Citation</span>2025</a></span>), we continue to stand up for and work toward these ideals. Those who continue to make changes in ways big and small wherever they are, like the projects and voices represented in this book, will lead the way regardless of political circumstance. When the fiery rhetoric has died down and the dust has settled in the aftermath of this latest iteration of white nationalism, the ongoing legacies of this work will be apparent, as it is with so much past DEIJ work.</p></div><div class="pb-dropzone" data-pb-dropzone="scholixLinksDropZone"><!-- Empty dropzone --></div></div><div class="pb-dropzone no-border-top" data-pb-dropzone="contentNavigationDropZoneFull"><div class="widget gql-content-navigation none  widget-none" id="d59557d1-e1fb-43ae-9542-192f8d2a53a7">

gold_text: How to Foster Diversity, Equity, Inclusion, and Justice in Geography As they prepared this volume in 2022, the coeditors could not have fathomed what would transpire in higher education in the United States in 2025: the relentless attacks on academic freedom and institutional independence; the systematic defunding, and thus the dismantling, of the well-respected U.S. research enterprise; and the weaponization of diversity, equity, inclusion, and justice (DEIJ) rhetorics among other things. Although elite higher educational institutions in the United States have borne the brunt of the Trump administration's attacks thus far, they reflect larger patterns of rising nationalisms across the globe that are attempting to tamp down free thought and the independence of educational institutions. Against this global political landscape, voices that bravely continue to advocate for DEIJ, like the ones proffered in this book, are all the more needed to combat the climate of intimidation and vulnerability. As this book is written by and for geographers, it serves as an important reminder that geography, as a discipline, has a responsibility and ethical imperative to use the scope of its resources-disciplinary knowledge, research tools, technological advancement and institutional and financial resources-to serve the needs of all of its members and protect those who are most marginal and at risk of being silenced. Geography and geographers must respond to global political threats in a timely, ethical manner. Of course, many subdisciplines in geography emerged precisely to address these concerns head on. Feminist, labor and postcolonial geographies, critical urban studies, and critical geographic information systems (GIS) have long produced impactful histories of interdisciplinary scholarship that have attended to questions of social inequality, power, and transformative change. Yet, decades of cutting-edge theorizing of race, gender, and other social differences have barely made a dent in improving the racial composition of the discipline. In one of the book's early chapters, Jordan and Raji point out that although gender representation has steadily increased in the discipline over the past couple of decades, undergraduates and graduate geography and geoscience programs are more than 80 percent white in the United States and the United Kingdom with very little change from previous decades. Furthermore, early career researchers of color in these fields face disproportionately lower levels of funding than white researchers. Troublingly, as I also learned through reading the book, Black and Latinx specialty groups have only been established a decade or so ago despite calls throughout the 1990s and early 2000s that highlighted this need (K. Davis, Nimoh, and Reason; Ybarra and Munoz). It raises the question as to why geography is slow to apply the discipline's radical thinking to the discipline itself. Coeditors Chen and Eaves write that "our goal [is] to create a growing community of theories and praxis for all interested in understanding, fostering, advancing, imagining, and envisioning a more diverse, equitable, inclusive, and just intellectual community of geography, including a space from which all under-represented geographers can speak" (p. 3). This book is an excellent starting place to learn about previous and ongoing DEIJ work in the discipline and unique projects building on these efforts. A strength of the book is the quality and range of the chapter contributions, and each chapter takes on a salient issue many geographers confront in their work, be it in their teaching, research, policy development, or efforts to promote institutional change, and explores a specific DEIJ-related issue within it. The focus spans the Anglo-American world with contributors from a range of backgrounds and identities hailing from the United Kingdom, North America, Southeast Asia, and the South Pacific. The chapter contributors probe the issues with thoughtfulness and depth, uncovering multilayered dimensions to the problems, and put forth novel ways of addressing them. Many of the contributors also thoughtfully acknowledge their own positionalities and locate themselves on a global spectrum to identify the intersecting layers of social privilege or marginality that shape their perspectives-an intentional effort to put DEIJ principles into practice. I walked away from reading this volume invigorated with fresh new ideas, tools, and additional resources to deepen both my DEIJ thinking and praxis as a geographer. The book is organized into three parts (or as a sequence of inquiries as the coeditors also put it): "Understanding DEI and Justice in Geography" ("what do we know?"); "Praxis and Examples of Fostering DEI and Justice in Geography" ("what can we do?"), and "Future of DEI and Justice in Geography: New Tools, Methods and Directions" ("what is next?"). Following the introduction, Chief Strategy Officer for the American Association of Geographers (AAG) Risha RaQuelle provides a framework for understanding institutional change and the ways the AAG has been advancing DEIJ goals since the murder of George Floyd, representing efforts to directly cultivate DEIJ at the disciplinary level in the United States. The subsequent first part "sets the epistemic and empirical foundations for DEI and justice in geography" (p. 5), and is the largest of the three subsequent parts. It consists of nine chapters, making up almost half the book. Most of the chapters that survey and locate the conversation in the discipline on a single axis of social grouping: Black, Latinx, Indigenous, Asian American, international, (dis-)abled and queer geographies, with the aforementioned chapter on the racial composition of geography and geoscience students in the United States and United Kingdom framing the part. My reaction to the chapter-by-chapter sequencing is a bit mixed: On the one hand, each chapter gets readers up to speed about the work being done in each of these subfields. Collectively, they make the important point about shifting the foci of DEIJ conversations from issues of representation, belonging, and procedural justice to ones of epistemology, knowledge creation, and analytic frameworks and methodologies, what Mei-Singh, Cheng, and Chen, borrowing from Shih (Citation2016), refer to as "epistemic justice." The chapters also highlight the challenges, as Anindita Datta puts it, of the intense emotional labor of "negotiating race, gender, and location in white field." Much of this work addresses what Settles and colleagues (Settles et al. Citation2021; Settles et al. Citation2022) referred to as "epistemic exclusion"-the way unconscious bias operates through the gatekeeping mechanisms of the academy. Epistemic justice aims to rectify the emotional exhaustion of epistemic exclusion by broadening the scope of epistemology and methodological tools to affirm cultural- or community-based ways of knowing. It is brilliantly illustrated in the chapter by Megan Ybarra and Lorena Munoz when they discuss their efforts to create a Latinx geographies specialty group (instead of an affinity group) within the AAG. At the same time, put together in this way, the chapters felt a bit schematic and not fully reflective of the complex, intersectional ways these categories play out in the real world. I caution against presenting social groups as neatly bounded categories because of the way they can be easily taken for granted by those less well-versed in DEIJ thought. The concepts of intersectionality, positionalities, and ambiguous identities are illustrated in individual chapters in this part and in subsequent chapters in the book, most poignantly in the chapter by Fitzgerald, Garrett, and Sharma. Given the part's length and centrality to the book, however, it would have been helpful if the coeditors discussed these concepts in more explicit terms to frame this part, perhaps through an introductory or concluding part that clarified the intersectional, overlapping nature of social identity categories. They do offer a bit of this analysis in the introduction, but it could be deepened and emphasized in the first part to ensure that the messiness and fluidity of these categories get reinforced there. Similarly, the part could benefit from an additional chapter on critical whiteness in geography. Focusing solely on marginalized or underrepresented groups makes it easy to assume that DEIJ advocacy is the responsibility of those most negatively affected by mainstream policies and practices-a conclusion easily drawn without examples that analyze white privilege. There are several chapters by geographers who identify as white and critically address the persistent whiteness in the discipline (e.g., through decolonial school geography in the United Kingdom, teaching geography courses from a social justice perspective at predominantly white institutions as a white instructor in the United States). An explicit chapter on critical whiteness in the epistemologically focused "what do we know?" part, however, might clarify how geography, as a discipline with roots in Western colonialism, resource extractivism, and imperialism, has been used to justify racial hierarchies and conquest of non-Western lands and cultures (Agnew and Duncan Citation2011). It has also been used in more contemporary racialized and racist land-use and spatial planning projects like redlining and urban decline (Aalbers Citation2014), the exploitation of "uninhabited" Native American lands (Sands Citation2011), and the justification of South African townships (Robinson Citation1997). Coming to terms with geography's complicity in the creation of systemic inequalities and social injustice means challenging the Eurocentric legacies underpinning much of mainstream geographical knowledge and practices. In drawing out these arguments, such a chapter could illustrate the ways that knowledge is not objective, neutral, and value-free; it is inherently racialized in the same ways whiteness is also racialized. This explanation could amplify the arguments made by the other contributors that highlight how culturally rooted, racialized epistemologies advance disciplinary knowledge in important-and historically overlooked-ways. The subsequent two parts, which make up another ten chapters and the second half of the book, cover specific ways in which DEIJ is being practiced in geography and give examples of tools that can be used to continue building on this work. A wide range of important topics are represented here, topics that need to be-but are rarely-addressed in ongoing professional development for geographers. In Part II ("what can we do?"), examples include decolonial and inclusive teaching methods as previously mentioned (Puttick and Cope), institutionalizing DEIJ policies and practices at the unit level (Skop and Li), and developing guidelines for safe, inclusive, and community-engaged field work (Alwan et al.). Part III ("what is next?") highlights a range of novel geographic tools and methodologies, like using GIS to map health inequalities (Jung); integrating (virtual) field work into teaching (York, Hurrell, and Hutchinson); and using games, podcasting, and crafting as tools for radical storytelling (H. A. Davis and Alderman), among others. The contributions in this part are grounded in praxis and real-world examples, so they address some of the messy, overlapping complexities I was seeking in the first part. At the same time, the authors helpfully discuss ways their projects could be adapted for other contexts and settings. Given how different each project is from one another, each part would benefit if the coeditors synthesized the chapters to explicitly identify key takeaways, general principles, or strategies "to practice DEIJ in geography," instead of leaving it to readers to deduce. One observation about the book as a whole is that it leans heavily toward the academic. Most (but not all) of the contributors have academic credentials and affiliations, and the approaches and topics might appeal most to academic geographers. Let me make two points about this: First, for a book that is academic in orientation, I might suggest discussing the ever-increasing corporatization of academic labor and the impacts of the resulting growing toxicity of academia as a profession on scholars from underrepresented backgrounds. There is a great deal of literature on this topic outside of geography (S. M. Davis Citation2024; Pittman Citation2025; Niemann, Gutiérrez y Muhs, and González Citation2020) and individual chapters in the first part do take some of this up (e.g., Fabris). Much of this literature discusses the isolation and "cultural tax" of being the sole faculty member from an underrepresented group in one's department or discipline and the increasingly extractive, dehumanizing nature of having one's scholarship and teaching measured by productivity metrics while working within increasingly bureaucratized institutions led by a disproportionate number of highly paid leaders from the managerial class (Slaughter and Rhoades Citation2004; Washburn Citation2008). The demographic cliff, institutional fiscal crises, rising student debt, and the global pandemic have only exacerbated these issues, all of which took place before the second election of Trump. In response, departments and disciplines are downsizing and merging, and institutions are shuttering in their entirety, creating an even greater scarcity of sustainable career options on the academic job market. As geographers from underrepresented groups, how do we navigate or even make sense of this terrain? How do we reestablish a sense of self and agency over our labor and find authentic support for our work? Is a career in academic geography even worth it? In a profession with a future that is so unpredictable, how do we advise graduate and undergraduate students, especially from similarly underrepresented backgrounds, who might want to emulate our career choices? It is heartbreaking to consider, but given factors affecting the profession overall, is it possible that steering students away from academia is a means to foster DEIJ in geography? There is a lot of room to discuss the ways scholars from underrepresented backgrounds in our discipline negotiate or push back against academia's unrelenting demands. Second, we need to broaden the conversation to include geographers outside of academic geography. Those adjacent to or outside of academic geography deserve to be served by these conversations as well. From my own experiences on the margins of academia (as a non-tenure-track lecturer), many nonacademic geographers do not feel they have a place in mainstream professional geography associations because of the perceived requirement that members focus heavily on research. Nonacademic geographers confront very different sets of DEIJ issues in their workplaces-issues that academics could possibly learn from, but that they, and the professional organizations that serve them, do not take up as often. If we are going to take inclusion seriously, we need to bring in voices and experiences outside the academic realm and similarly expand support by our professional associations. What does DEIJ look like for someone who teaches AP Human Geography at an urban high school? Or for a federal worker who is no longer permitted to use the language of "diversity, equity and inclusion" in their workplace? Or for someone who is head of a food justice nonprofit or an entrepreneur running her own GIS consulting firm? Incorporating these perspectives can showcase the diverse range of professions in which geographers work while bringing in different sets of questions, concerns and analytical lenses to DEIJ in geography. In turn, it also broadens what DEIJ in geography looks like and who is served by this profession. Overall, How to Foster Diversity, Equity, Inclusion, and Justice in Geography is an excellent starting place for learning and garnering ideas about how to put these values into practice in our field. It helped me think more deeply about how we can widen the scope of inclusion and justice in our field, some suggestions about which I have offered here. Clearly, in the current political climate, expanding knowledge and praxis under the banner of DEIJ will be harder to achieve. Although we might change the name, the framing, or the approach of what we do, it is important that, unlike the corporations and institutions who preemptively shed their commitments to DEIJ in the wake of Trump's second election (Naidu and Jessop Citation2025), we continue to stand up for and work toward these ideals. Those who continue to make changes in ways big and small wherever they are, like the projects and voices represented in this book, will lead the way regardless of political circumstance. When the fiery rhetoric has died down and the dust has settled in the aftermath of this latest iteration of white nationalism, the ongoing legacies of this work will be apparent, as it is with so much past DEIJ work.

                            <div class="hlFld-Fulltext"><div id="abstractId1" class="hlFld-Abstract"><h2 class="section-heading-2" id="abstract">ABSTRACT</h2><p class="last">In 1887, psychical researchers Richard Hodgson and S. J. Davey published a study that revealed counterintuitive aspects of human cognition: How healthy, sober, honest observers of events can be prone to seemingly remarkable errors of eyewitness testimony. Their report, titled ‘The Possibilities of Mal-Observation and Lapse of Memory from a Practical Point of View’ included a collection of eyewitness statements from participants in a series of hoax séances. Hodgson and Davey asserted that all phenomena in their séances were produced using techniques drawn from performance magic. However, their participants were not initially informed about this fact. In their accounts, participants consistently attributed events that they saw, not to trickery, but to spiritual phenomena and psychic powers on the part of Davey, who played the role of the ‘medium’. A major advantage this novel paradigm was that the experimenters had a highly reliable record of actual events, because they had orchestrated the séances themselves. Their paper emphasised the contrasts between what their participants reported remembering relative to what had actually occurred. The errors of the witnesses were marked by failures to notice or remember key aspects of the séance, and even instances where the participants seemed to confabulate- confidently reporting events that had never really taken place. Neither Hodgson nor Davey would have identified themselves as psychologists or cognitive scientists, rather they considered themselves to be psychical researchers, operating under the auspices of the Society for Psychical Research (SPR). At the time, experimental psychology was only just beginning to emerge as a formal and distinct academic discipline. But looking back on their work from a modern perspective, it arguably anticipated more formal theoretical and empirical developments in cognitive psychology by decades. Ironically, given that their report systematically documented failures of attention and lapses of memory, it has been largely ignored in historical considerations of psychology research and is relatively unknown today. In this paper, I will explore the historical context of Hodgson and Davey’s report and discuss how some of their key findings can be related to our contemporary scientific understanding of attention, memory, metacognition, and the science of magic.</p></div><div class="abstractKeywords"><div class="hlFld-KeywordText"><div><p id="kwd-title-d2983901e99" class="kwd-title">KEYWORDS: </p><ul aria-labelledby="kwd-title-d2983901e99"><li><a href="/keyword/Attention" class="kwd-btn keyword-click" kameleoonlistener-jeqi="true">Attention</a></li><li><a href="/keyword/memory" class="kwd-btn keyword-click" kameleoonlistener-quel="true">memory</a></li><li><a href="/keyword/eyewitness+testimony" class="kwd-btn keyword-click" kameleoonlistener-5qyl="true">eyewitness testimony</a></li><li><a href="/keyword/psychical+research" class="kwd-btn keyword-click" kameleoonlistener-v2pp="true">psychical research</a></li><li><a href="/keyword/science+of+magic" class="kwd-btn keyword-click" kameleoonlistener-xtgx="true">science of magic</a></li><li><a href="/keyword/illusion" class="kwd-btn keyword-click" kameleoonlistener-cyud="true">illusion</a></li></ul></div></div></div><div id="embedded-pdf-target" class="with-border"></div><div class="pb-dropzone" data-pb-dropzone="contentNavigationDropZoneAbs"><div class="widget gql-content-navigation none  widget-none" id="2ffb43c7-15dc-4c79-9e29-8e4bed9b3d1e">
        
        

        <div class="wrapped ">
            
            <div class="widget-body body body-none "><div class="ajaxWidget" data-ajax-widget="gql-content-navigation" data-ajax-widget-id="2ffb43c7-15dc-4c79-9e29-8e4bed9b3d1e" data-ajax-observe="true">
    
</div></div>
        </div>
    </div></div><div class="NLM_sec NLM_sec_level_1" id="s0001"><h2 class="section-heading-2" id="d1e120">Introduction</h2><p>In 1887, psychical researchers Richard Hodgson and S. J. Davey published a report detailing a series of experiments designed to examine the reliability of eyewitness testimony.<span class="ref-lnk lazy-ref en"><a data-rid="en0001" href="#" data-behaviour="toggle-ref" data-ref-type="fn" data-label="footnote"><span class="off-screen">Footnote</span><sup>1</sup></a></span> Their article, ‘The Possibilities of Mal-observation and Lapse of Memory from a Practical Point of View’, (referred to throughout this paper as the Mal-Observation Report) describes how they conducted a series of performances using sleight-of-hand methods to apparently demonstrate supernatural communication with the spirits of the dead. Before explaining that the effects were tricks, they asked their participants to produce written accounts of what they remembered. These written accounts revealed that the participants reliably misperceived and misremembered key aspects of the performances, with many of them being unable to explain the real methods behind the trick and resorting to supernatural explanations. Not only is this one of the first recorded instances of studying participants’ reactions to sleight-of-hand magic tricks, but it is arguably one of the earliest experimental psychological accounts of phenomena now known as reconstructive memory and inattentional blindness, which Hodgson and Davey referred to at the time as <i>mal-observation</i>. Both reconstructive memory and inattentional blindness are concepts that did not receive formal labels or widespread scientific recognition until many years after Hodgson and Davey’s report. Today, the term ‘reconstructive memory’ refers to the concept that our ability to recall past events involves an active reconstruction based on our general knowledge, assumptions, and expectations, as opposed to simply being a faithful reproduction of past experiences.<span class="ref-lnk lazy-ref en"><a data-rid="en0002" href="#" data-behaviour="toggle-ref" data-ref-type="fn" data-label="footnote"><span class="off-screen">Footnote</span><sup>2</sup></a></span> A reconstructive memory process <i>can</i> result in accurate memories, but a direct consequence of this reconstructive process is that it is prone to errors and false recollections. Traditionally, psychologists attribute the initial theoretical conceptualisation of reconstructive memory to the work of Fredrick Bartlett, a psychologist who is credited with pioneering formal investigations on human memory outside of laboratory settings.<span class="ref-lnk lazy-ref en"><a data-rid="en0003" href="#" data-behaviour="toggle-ref" data-ref-type="fn" data-label="footnote"><span class="off-screen">Footnote</span><sup>3</sup></a></span> Subsequently, another key body of experimental and theoretical literature on reconstructive memory is attributed to the works of Elizabeth Loftus, which, since the 1970s, empirically demonstrated that reconstructive processes can yield significant and long-lasting changes to reported memories, including the generation of ‘false memories’ – elaborate recollections for events that never actually occurred but are phenomenologically indistinguishable from ‘true’ memories of events that genuinely occurred.<span class="ref-lnk lazy-ref en"><a data-rid="en0004" href="#" data-behaviour="toggle-ref" data-ref-type="fn" data-label="footnote"><span class="off-screen">Footnote</span><sup>4</sup></a></span> Another phenomenon that would not be formally recognised until decades later, but is nonetheless evident in Hodgson and Davey’s report, is ‘inattentional blindness’. This term describes the fact that we can fail to detect visual objects or events that are fully visible and in plain sight when our attention is otherwise engaged. The term first emerged in the 1990s, when psychologists Mack and Rock reported a series of experiments, wherein they used simple computerised visual displays to demonstrate that participants would often fail to notice obvious visual stimuli.<span class="ref-lnk lazy-ref en"><a data-rid="en0005" href="#" data-behaviour="toggle-ref" data-ref-type="fn" data-label="footnote"><span class="off-screen">Footnote</span><sup>5</sup></a></span> Later studies have demonstrated that inattentional blindness is not limited to failures to notice simple shapes on a computer monitor, but can also occur in more naturalistic, complex, and dynamic scenes.<span class="ref-lnk lazy-ref en"><a data-rid="en0006" href="#" data-behaviour="toggle-ref" data-ref-type="fn" data-label="footnote"><span class="off-screen">Footnote</span><sup>6</sup></a></span> Both reconstructive memory and inattentional blindness are deeply counterintuitive psychological concepts that <i>seem</i> to contradict everyday human experience.<span class="ref-lnk lazy-ref en"><a data-rid="en0007" href="#" data-behaviour="toggle-ref" data-ref-type="fn" data-label="footnote"><span class="off-screen">Footnote</span><sup>7</sup></a></span> It <i>feels</i> impossible that we can generate real-seeming memories of events that never happened, or that we can fail to see seemingly obvious visual events that occur right before our eyes. Such disconnections between how people <i>feel</i> cognition works, and how it actually functions can be classified as metacognitive illusions. Thanks to a large body of careful empirical work that accumulated throughout the twentieth century, inattentional blindness and reconstructive memory are now firmly established to be a natural part of healthy everyday human cognitive processes. But despite the fact that the Hodgson and Davey’s 1887 report systematically described many of these phenomena, it is generally overlooked, aside from rather specialised publications related to magic illusions, anomalistic psychology, or parapsychology.<span class="ref-lnk lazy-ref en"><a data-rid="en0008" href="#" data-behaviour="toggle-ref" data-ref-type="fn" data-label="footnote"><span class="off-screen">Footnote</span><sup>8</sup></a></span> According to Google Scholar (accessed 14 August 2025), Hodgson and Davey’s report has been cited a total of only 70 times. In contrast, Fredric Bartlett’s <i>Remembering</i> has been cited 28,682 times, Elizabeth Loftus’ most cited review chapter related to false memory formation has been cited 5218 times, and Daniel Simons and Christopher Chabris’ iconic study of inattentional blindness has been cited 4691 times. <span class="ref-lnk lazy-ref en"><a data-rid="en0009" href="#" data-behaviour="toggle-ref" data-ref-type="fn" data-label="footnote"><span class="off-screen">Footnote</span><sup>9</sup></a></span> In this paper, I aim to make the case that Hodgson and Davey’s Mal-Observation Report is well worth remembering and attending.</p><div class="NLM_sec NLM_sec_level_2" id="s0001-s2001"><h3 class="section-heading-3" id="d1e171">Setting the Stage</h3><p>The Mal-Observation Report was published at a confluence of three historically parallel trends: The rise of ‘Modern Spiritualism’, the popularity of performance magic as entertainment, and the emergence of experimental psychology as a formal scientific and academic discipline.<span class="ref-lnk lazy-ref en"><a data-rid="en0010" href="#" data-behaviour="toggle-ref" data-ref-type="fn" data-label="footnote"><span class="off-screen">Footnote</span><sup>10</sup></a></span> Modern Spiritualism refers to a socio-cultural religious movement that spread throughout the US and around the world, starting in the mid-1800s. Many religious practices promote the idea that a person’s spirit or soul survives beyond death, but spiritualism set itself apart from more conventional religions in that proponents asserted that the spirits of the dead could physically interact and directly communicate with the living. Furthermore, the miracles of Modern Spiritualism were not relegated to stories of ancient texts, rather they were presented as contemporary, participatory, and, above all, empirical. Anyone could personally witness proof of spiritualistic phenomena; no faith was required.</p><p>As spiritualistic practices spread and flourished in popularity, spiritualistic phenomena allegedly manifested in variety of ways. Early mediums, like the Fox Sisters initially claimed communicated with spirits through ‘raps’ or knocking noises.<span class="ref-lnk lazy-ref en"><a data-rid="en0011" href="#" data-behaviour="toggle-ref" data-ref-type="fn" data-label="footnote"><span class="off-screen">Footnote</span><sup>11</sup></a></span> But alternative and more spectacular methods of demonstrating spiritual phenomena rapidly proliferated. In the most extreme instances of physical phenomena, spirits were said to visibly manifest in plain view as disembodied faces, hands, or full bodies. Or the spirits might invisibly hoist objects and musical instruments. Spiritualist mediums would claim to ‘channel’ spirits that could provide them with extraordinary abilities, such as access to knowledge that they had no earthly way of knowing or allow them to perform physically impossible feats like levitation.<span class="ref-lnk lazy-ref en"><a data-rid="en0012" href="#" data-behaviour="toggle-ref" data-ref-type="fn" data-label="footnote"><span class="off-screen">Footnote</span><sup>12</sup></a></span> New modalities of spirit communication likewise emerged. Such methods included table tilting, wherein invisible spirits would appear to shake small tables. In other instances, the spirits might engage in direct voice communication wherein they would speak through the voices of the medium. Sometimes the spirits would cause levitations of objects or even the mediums themselves. Of particular relevance to the present discussion was the practice of ‘psychography’ or independent slate-writing.<span class="ref-lnk lazy-ref en"><a data-rid="en0013" href="#" data-behaviour="toggle-ref" data-ref-type="fn" data-label="footnote"><span class="off-screen">Footnote</span><sup>13</sup></a></span> In slate-writing séances, the medium would present participants with one or more school slates — small handheld blackboards that were of common use by schoolchildren at that time (<button class="ref show-table-fig-ref" data-id="f0001" data-behaviour="show-popup" data-popup-event-type="fig">Figure 1</button>). The slates would be shown to be free of any marks. And then, under circumstances where it would seem that no one could have physically written on the slates, writing would appear. Such writings were attributed to spirit agency.
</p><div class="figureView"><div class="short-legend"><p class="captionText"><span aria-level="3" role="heading"><span class="captionLabel">Figure 1. </span></span> Example of an ‘ungimmicked’ school slate. This slate was used by upstate New York school children in the late 19<sup>th</sup> or early 20<sup>th</sup> Century.<span class="ref-lnk lazy-ref en"><a data-rid="en0014" href="#" data-behaviour="toggle-ref" data-ref-type="fn" data-label="footnote"><span class="off-screen">Footnote</span><sup>14</sup></a></span>.</p></div><a href="#" class="thumbnail" data-behaviour="show-popup" data-popup-event-type="fig" data-id="f0001"><img id="d1e205" src="/cms/asset/42a80338-95d0-4946-bd4d-b458bfd37885/ranr_a_2579758_f0001_oc.jpg" loading="lazy" height="500" width="374" alt="Figure 1. Example of an ‘ungimmicked’ school slate. This slate was used by upstate New York school children in the late 19th or early 20th Century.Footnote14."></a><div><button class="show-full-size btn btn-sm" data-behaviour="show-popup" data-id="f0001" data-popup-event-type="fig">Display full size</button></div></div><p></p><p>Several slate-writing mediums achieved celebrity status, making them of particular interest to both the general public and the scientific community. One of the most notorious slate-writing mediums was Dr. Henry Slade. Slade was an American spirit medium who began his career as a ‘clairvoyant physician’ (his title of doctor was not attributable to any academic or medical institution), but he would go on to become internationally famous for his propensity for producing slate-written communications from spirits.<span class="ref-lnk lazy-ref en"><a data-rid="en0015" href="#" data-behaviour="toggle-ref" data-ref-type="fn" data-label="footnote"><span class="off-screen">Footnote</span><sup>15</sup></a></span> This skillset led him to travel extensively around the world. While visiting London in 1877, he was arrested and tried for fraud.<span class="ref-lnk lazy-ref en"><a data-rid="en0016" href="#" data-behaviour="toggle-ref" data-ref-type="fn" data-label="footnote"><span class="off-screen">Footnote</span><sup>16</sup></a></span> The trial drew international attention and ended with Slade being convicted of fraud, but then having his conviction overturned on a legal technicality. He fled Britain before he could be re-tried, eventually ending up in Leipzig Germany, where he demonstrated his powers to luminaries from the field psychophysics (a precursor of experimental psychology), including Gustav Fechner, Johann Zöllner, the university’s chair of astrophysics, and Wilhelm Wundt, who would later be dubbed the founding father of experimental psychology.<span class="ref-lnk lazy-ref en"><a data-rid="en0017" href="#" data-behaviour="toggle-ref" data-ref-type="fn" data-label="footnote"><span class="off-screen">Footnote</span><sup>17</sup></a></span> Over the course of multiple sittings over several weeks, Slade not only demonstrated slate-writing but a variety of phenomena that were (seemingly) unexplainable by conventional physical laws, including the deflection of a compass needle with his mind, tying impossible knots in string, materialising and dematerialising small objects, clairvoyance, and even the manifestation of a tangible spirit hand. Zöllner was impressed with Slade’s abilities, so much so that he proposed a new scientific discipline of <i>Transcendentale Physik</i> [Transcendental Physics] to explain Slade’s mediumship in terms of fourth dimensional geometry.<span class="ref-lnk lazy-ref en"><a data-rid="en0018" href="#" data-behaviour="toggle-ref" data-ref-type="fn" data-label="footnote"><span class="off-screen">Footnote</span><sup>18</sup></a></span> Zöllner rushed to publish his findings and theories as a multi-volume set of <i>Wissenschaftliche Abhandlungen</i> (‘Scientific Papers’ published from 1877–1878), which contained more than 2000 pages describing his investigations of Slade. The writings stirred controversy not only in Germany but around the world.<span class="ref-lnk lazy-ref en"><a data-rid="en0019" href="#" data-behaviour="toggle-ref" data-ref-type="fn" data-label="footnote"><span class="off-screen">Footnote</span><sup>19</sup></a></span> In 1880, Charles Carleton Massesy, a British barrister, compiled and translated selections of Zöllner’s German writings and published them under the title <i>Transcendental Physics</i>—the book proved to be popular, particularly with English-speaking spiritualists, and was republished in multiple editions. <span class="ref-lnk lazy-ref en"><a data-rid="en0020" href="#" data-behaviour="toggle-ref" data-ref-type="fn" data-label="footnote"><span class="off-screen">Footnote</span><sup>20</sup></a></span> Crucially, Zöllner was aware of accusations that Slade was dishonest, but he asserted that Slade was an honest man who was being unfairly slandered by small-minded people.<span class="ref-lnk lazy-ref en"><a data-rid="en0021" href="#" data-behaviour="toggle-ref" data-ref-type="fn" data-label="footnote"><span class="off-screen">Footnote</span><sup>21</sup></a></span> One such person was Wilhelm Wundt, who had been invited to witness one of Slade’s demonstrations, published an open letter asserting that Slade’s demonstrations could be more rationally dismissed as ‘jugglery’ or sleight-of-hand magic methods.<span class="ref-lnk lazy-ref en"><a data-rid="en0022" href="#" data-behaviour="toggle-ref" data-ref-type="fn" data-label="footnote"><span class="off-screen">Footnote</span><sup>22</sup></a></span> However, despite rhetorically gesturing towards the idea of magic trick methods, Wundt, as a non-magician himself, did not offer any substantive methodological explanations for how Slade might have accomplished such convincing tricks. Zöllner continued to promote Transcendental Physics until his death in 1882, while Wundt went on to establish the world’s first-ever formally recognised laboratory of experimental psychology at Leipzig in 1883.<span class="ref-lnk lazy-ref en"><a data-rid="en0023" href="#" data-behaviour="toggle-ref" data-ref-type="fn" data-label="footnote"><span class="off-screen">Footnote</span><sup>23</sup></a></span></p><p>In developing his lab and legacy, Wundt never returned to investigations of magic and spiritual fraud. Arguably, his and other psychologists’ disengagement from psychical research represented a deliberate strategic effort to distance the nascent field of experimental psychology from associations with spiritual phenomena.<span class="ref-lnk lazy-ref en"><a data-rid="en0024" href="#" data-behaviour="toggle-ref" data-ref-type="fn" data-label="footnote"><span class="off-screen">Footnote</span><sup>24</sup></a></span> But other researchers were more eager to explore both magic tricks and the scientific claims associated with the modern spiritualism movement. In 1882, a group of scholars in Cambridge banded together to form the Society for Psychical Research (SPR), with the goal of investigating phenomena associated with the spiritualist movement. The membership came to include scientific luminaries like Alfred Russell Wallace, William Crookes, William James, and Oliver Lodge. The SPR was specifically established to engage with spiritualist claims, including mediumship, apparitional experiences, haunted houses, and the survival of the soul after bodily death. The SPR’s main mechanism for disseminating its findings was through printed publications. The society produced a monthly <i>Journal of the Society for Psychical Research</i> that was intended exclusively to members, and they also produced a public facing series of <i>Proceedings of the Society of Psychical Research</i>, which were intended for public consumption. The exact nature of the SPR’s distribution numbers in the 1880s are not explicitly documented in contemporary publications of their <i>Journal</i> or <i>Proceedings</i>. However, in a recorded speech given in 1885 by the SPR’s then president, Balfour Stewart, he remarked that:
</p><div class="quote"><p class="first last">In reply to the question, what has the Society done? I may state that since its commencement it has issued seven parts of <i>Proceedings</i>, of which a total number exceeding 12,000 has been distributed to Members and others, placed in public libraries, sent for review, and sold through the ordinary channels.<span class="ref-lnk lazy-ref en"><a data-rid="en0025" href="#" data-behaviour="toggle-ref" data-ref-type="fn" data-label="footnote"><span class="off-screen">Footnote</span><sup>25</sup></a></span></p></div><p></p><p>Advertisements for the SPR’s <i>Proceedings</i> could be found in regional newspapers. For example, the issue of the <i>Proceedings</i> featuring the Mal-Observation Report could be ordered by anyone for the price of 4 shillings<span class="ref-lnk lazy-ref en"><a data-rid="en0026" href="#" data-behaviour="toggle-ref" data-ref-type="fn" data-label="footnote"><span class="off-screen">Footnote</span><sup>26</sup></a></span> (<button class="ref show-table-fig-ref" data-id="f0002" data-behaviour="show-popup" data-popup-event-type="fig">Figure 2</button>), about 25 pounds or 29 euros in today’s currency<span class="ref-lnk lazy-ref en"><a data-rid="en0027" href="#" data-behaviour="toggle-ref" data-ref-type="fn" data-label="footnote"><span class="off-screen">Footnote</span><sup>27</sup></a></span> (Bank of England, <span class="ref-lnk lazy-ref bibr"><a data-rid="cit0004" href="#" data-behaviour="toggle-ref" data-ref-type="bibr" data-label="reference"><span class="off-screen">Citation</span>2025</a></span>). The SPR members’ methods of communicating their findings and discussions through printed media, both internally and externally, arguably reveal important patterns in the ways that researchers have presented debates about scientific developments. The impacts of the practices were not limited to the domain of paranormal studies: Lamont identifies these scientific debates around spiritualism as a Victorian <i>crisis of evidence</i> that would directly shape the development of modern conventions of academic psychology.<span class="ref-lnk lazy-ref en"><a data-rid="en0028" href="#" data-behaviour="toggle-ref" data-ref-type="fn" data-label="footnote"><span class="off-screen">Footnote</span><sup>28</sup></a></span> Similarly, Efram Sera-Shriar has identified the SPR’s debates around <i>credible witnessing</i> – the question of who has the authority to make qualified observations of extraordinary phenomena — as re-shaping academic conventions of anthropology. <span class="ref-lnk lazy-ref en"><a data-rid="en0029" href="#" data-behaviour="toggle-ref" data-ref-type="fn" data-label="footnote"><span class="off-screen">Footnote</span><sup>29</sup></a></span> Furthermore, Noakes has demonstrated how such debates and investigations influenced the modern practice of physics. <span class="ref-lnk lazy-ref en"><a data-rid="en0030" href="#" data-behaviour="toggle-ref" data-ref-type="fn" data-label="footnote"><span class="off-screen">Footnote</span><sup>30</sup></a></span>
</p><div class="figureView"><div class="short-legend"><p class="captionText"><span aria-level="3" role="heading"><span class="captionLabel">Figure 2. </span></span> Image of a Publishers Column advertising the issue of the SPR’s <i>Proceedings</i> featuring Hodgson and Davey’s Mal-Observation Report<span class="ref-lnk lazy-ref en"><a data-rid="en0031" href="#" data-behaviour="toggle-ref" data-ref-type="fn" data-label="footnote"><span class="off-screen">Footnote</span><sup>31</sup></a></span>.</p></div><a href="#" class="thumbnail" data-behaviour="show-popup" data-popup-event-type="fig" data-id="f0002"><img id="d1e322" src="/cms/asset/46726c3f-84df-4baf-8f31-b14f9b7e26e1/ranr_a_2579758_f0002_b.gif" loading="lazy" height="500" width="489" alt="Figure 2. Image of a Publishers Column advertising the issue of the SPR’s Proceedings featuring Hodgson and Davey’s Mal-Observation ReportFootnote31."></a><div><button class="show-full-size btn btn-sm" data-behaviour="show-popup" data-id="f0002" data-popup-event-type="fig">Display full size</button></div></div><p></p><p>Partially as a result of Henry Slade’s notoriety, the SPR became particularly concerned with the practice of psychography, and the value of evidence obtained by testimonies of this extraordinary phenomenon. Hodgson and Davey’s Mal-Observation Report was largely inspired by controversies related to eyewitness accounts of slate-writing séances. They were concerned, not only with accounts of Slade’s feats, but also with the alleged phenomena of William Eglinton,<span class="ref-lnk lazy-ref en"><a data-rid="en0032" href="#" data-behaviour="toggle-ref" data-ref-type="fn" data-label="footnote"><span class="off-screen">Footnote</span><sup>32</sup></a></span> a British medium who developed his own reputation for slate-writing after Slade had fled England following his trial for fraud. The SPR received and published numerous accounts of extraordinary test sittings from various members of the public who had witnessed Eglinton in action.<span class="ref-lnk lazy-ref en"><a data-rid="en0033" href="#" data-behaviour="toggle-ref" data-ref-type="fn" data-label="footnote"><span class="off-screen">Footnote</span><sup>33</sup></a></span> Eglinton would use slates that had been provided by the witness, and having placed a small piece of chalk between two blank slates, would produce messages. These were words selected by the participants, sometimes seemingly randomly chosen books that Eglinton had apparently no way of seeing. Frank Podmore, one of the SPR’s founding members wrote, in 1902, that ‘In the history of the movement, no physical manifestation had ever won such universal recognition’ as Eglinton’s abilities.<span class="ref-lnk lazy-ref en"><a data-rid="en0034" href="#" data-behaviour="toggle-ref" data-ref-type="fn" data-label="footnote"><span class="off-screen">Footnote</span><sup>34</sup></a></span> Accounts of Eglinton’s mediumship sparked a fiery debate in the pages of the SPR’s publications. Eleanor Mildred Sidgwick published a sceptical paper cautioning that the Society should never seriously consider accounts of mediums who have ever been credibly accused of fraud, and she specifically accused Eglinton of having been caught faking manifestations. She wrote that he had been caught with props, including muslin drapes and a false beard that were clearly intended to be used for creating hoax apparitions. Sidgwick attributed the remarkable accounts of his activities to a combination of conjuring (i.e., magic trick) methods being deployed by the medium and ‘mal-observation’ on the part of witnesses (i.e., perceptual and memory illusions).<span class="ref-lnk lazy-ref en"><a data-rid="en0035" href="#" data-behaviour="toggle-ref" data-ref-type="fn" data-label="footnote"><span class="off-screen">Footnote</span><sup>35</sup></a></span> Her sceptical assertions were met with a scepticism on the part of Eglinton’s supporters. Charles Carleton Massey (who had produced the English translations of Zöllner’s investigations of Henry Slade) directly responded to Sidgwick by asserting that mal-observation could not possibly account for the phenomena allegedly produced by Eglinton. ‘Most of us would feel ashamed’, he wrote, ‘of mistaking a conjurer’s trick for a genuine manifestation of unknown force’.<span class="ref-lnk lazy-ref en"><a data-rid="en0036" href="#" data-behaviour="toggle-ref" data-ref-type="fn" data-label="footnote"><span class="off-screen">Footnote</span><sup>36</sup></a></span> Magicians, he wrote, could only accomplish their deceptions under conditions that were highly inferior to that of a test medium. According to Massey, in séances, participants generally knew exactly what phenomena were going to be produced. Magicians, he argued, would be unable to successfully perform illusion if their audiences were aware of exactly what tricks they would be performing; such uncertainty ‘does not and cannot exist’.<span class="ref-lnk lazy-ref en"><a data-rid="en0037" href="#" data-behaviour="toggle-ref" data-ref-type="fn" data-label="footnote"><span class="off-screen">Footnote</span><sup>37</sup></a></span> If deception was possible for Eglinton during his slate-writing séances, Massey argued that the only reasonable conclusion would be that all accounts based on human observation would have to be considered ‘absolutely worthless’.<span class="ref-lnk lazy-ref en"><a data-rid="en0038" href="#" data-behaviour="toggle-ref" data-ref-type="fn" data-label="footnote"><span class="off-screen">Footnote</span><sup>38</sup></a></span> He appealed to his readers to consider that the witnesses to Eglinton (and other mediums) could not be so easily fooled. While he acknowledged that an honest witness might sometimes forget certain facts and events, he argued that they could never honestly ‘<i>invent</i> specific and positive events of perception’.<span class="ref-lnk lazy-ref en"><a data-rid="en0039" href="#" data-behaviour="toggle-ref" data-ref-type="fn" data-label="footnote"><span class="off-screen">Footnote</span><sup>39</sup></a></span> Massey’s sentiments were representative of other scientists who espoused the validity and importance of spiritualistic phenomena. For example, Alfred Russell Wallace, a scientific luminary in the field of biology, known for co-developing the theory of natural selection along with Charles Darwin, had written that the miracles of spiritualism had ‘been tested and examined by sceptics of every grade of incredulity, men in every way qualified to detect imposture or discover natural causes- trained physicists, medical men, lawyers, and men of business- but in every case the investigators have retired baffled, or become converts’.<span class="ref-lnk lazy-ref en"><a data-rid="en0040" href="#" data-behaviour="toggle-ref" data-ref-type="fn" data-label="footnote"><span class="off-screen">Footnote</span><sup>40</sup></a></span></p><p class="last">In response to this line of argumentation, Sidgwick turned to Angelo John Lewis, a barrister and a semi-professional magician who performed and wrote under the stage name Professor Hoffmann. Lewis not only examined written accounts by Eglinton’s witnesses, but also personally attended twelve sittings with Eglinton. In describing his analysis of the witness accounts of Eglinton’s phenomena<span class="ref-lnk lazy-ref en"><a data-rid="en0041" href="#" data-behaviour="toggle-ref" data-ref-type="fn" data-label="footnote"><span class="off-screen">Footnote</span>41</a></span><sup>,</sup><span class="ref-lnk lazy-ref en"><a data-rid="en0042" href="#" data-behaviour="toggle-ref" data-ref-type="fn" data-label="footnote"><span class="off-screen">Footnote</span><sup>42</sup></a></span>, Lewis was careful to acknowledge that he was open to the possibility of genuine spiritual phenomena, but wrote that in his opinion as a magician, the witness accounts were indeed suggestive of errors of observation that might be attributable to conjuring deceptions. He noted that witnesses to magic performances did not necessarily describe events that they saw, but rather events that they imagined they saw. He also acknowledged that even highly trained magicians could still be fooled by conjuring methods that they were not personally familiar with or not expecting. As to Lewis’ personal experiences sitting with Eglinton, it transpired that throughout repeated attempts ‘the spirits obstinately declined to manifest’. Such blank séances presented the debating researchers with something of a rhetorical stalemate. Proponents of spiritualism could argue that the uneventful sittings were evidence in favour of the genuineness of mediums, after all, if the medium was resorting to conjuring then, surely, they would always be able to perform their tricks. And thus, the unreliability of their mediumship supported the idea that reported spiritual phenomena were logically attributable to forces outside of the mediums’ direct control. On the other hand, sceptics could argue that fraudulent mediums would deliberately avoid using trickery if they suspected they were being observed by a sitter with conjuring expertise (as Lewis was well known for). And the medium could simply wait to perform their deceptions until they were in the presence of a more gullible audience, while claiming that the blank séances were outside their control.</p></div></div><div class="NLM_sec NLM_sec_level_1" id="s0002"><h2 class="section-heading-2" id="d1e365">Hodgson and Davey’s Mal-Observation Report</h2><p>Hodgson and Davey’s Mal-Observation Report describes a scientific investigation that they developed as a way of around the empirical problem of investigating the reliability of testimonies related allegedly genuine spiritualist mediumship. By using magic trick methods to simulate slate-writing phenomena, they avoided the problem of blank séances that had plagued Lewis’ investigation. Furthermore, by relying exclusively on magic trick methods performed by an openly <i>fake</i> medium who made no claim to supernormal abilities, they (vainly) hoped to avoid the potential criticism that any genuine psychical phenomena might occur during their experiments. Hodgson took care to declare that even though the participants testimonies might seem ‘marvellous enough’ to support the hypothesis of occult agency, ‘the “psychographic” phenomena described in the following records are conjuring, and only conjuring, performances’.<span class="ref-lnk lazy-ref en"><a data-rid="en0043" href="#" data-behaviour="toggle-ref" data-ref-type="fn" data-label="footnote"><span class="off-screen">Footnote</span><sup>43</sup></a></span> ‘The object of the notes’, he wrote, was not to educate readers about particular conjuring methods, but ‘to show to investigators the kind and degree of mistakes which may be made by educated and intelligent witnesses in recording their impression of a performance the main lines of which are planned with the deliberate intention of deceiving them, but few, if any, of the details of which can be described as absolutely fixed’.<span class="ref-lnk lazy-ref en"><a data-rid="en0044" href="#" data-behaviour="toggle-ref" data-ref-type="fn" data-label="footnote"><span class="off-screen">Footnote</span><sup>44</sup></a></span></p><p>The Mal-Observation Report represents the synthesis of Hodgson’s first-hand experience debunking professional mediums and Davey’s conjuring expertise. Richard Hodgson (<button class="ref show-table-fig-ref" data-id="f0003" data-behaviour="show-popup" data-popup-event-type="fig">Figure 3</button>) was born in Melbourne, Australia and obtained a degree in Law from Cambridge University.<span class="ref-lnk lazy-ref en"><a data-rid="en0046" href="#" data-behaviour="toggle-ref" data-ref-type="fn" data-label="footnote"><span class="off-screen">Footnote</span><sup>46</sup></a></span> During his time at Cambridge, Hodgson joined the recently formed SPR. As a member of the society, Hodgson had developed reputation as a talented detective debunker of spiritualist mediums. He spearheaded one of the SPR’s first major investigations into spiritualism when he travelled to India to investigate Countess Helena Petrova de Blavatsky, a Russian occultist who had attracted a significant following based on her alleged supernatural abilities. As a founder of the Theosophy movement, Blavatsky claimed that she was directly channelling the spiritual teachings of dead mystics to develop what has variously been described as an occult or new religious system.<span class="ref-lnk lazy-ref en"><a data-rid="en0047" href="#" data-behaviour="toggle-ref" data-ref-type="fn" data-label="footnote"><span class="off-screen">Footnote</span><sup>47</sup></a></span> Hodgson spent two months in India attempting to verify Blavatsky’s claims. In his eventual report, which he published through the SPR in 1885, he declared that the phenomena that she claimed credit for were entirely fraudulent.<span class="ref-lnk lazy-ref en"><a data-rid="en0048" href="#" data-behaviour="toggle-ref" data-ref-type="fn" data-label="footnote"><span class="off-screen">Footnote</span><sup>48</sup></a></span> According to Hodgson, the letters Blavatsky claimed to receive from spirits of the dead were written in her own hand, and the spirit forms she manifested were simply human accomplices wearing disguises. Hodgson asserted that Blavatsky’s followers were ‘excessively credulous and deficient in observation’, and that she was actually the centre of a ‘huge fraudulent system’.<span class="ref-lnk lazy-ref en"><a data-rid="en0049" href="#" data-behaviour="toggle-ref" data-ref-type="fn" data-label="footnote"><span class="off-screen">Footnote</span><sup>49</sup></a></span> Hodgson’s experiences investigating Blavatsky arguably helped spark his initial interest in the relationship between magic tricks and eyewitness testimony, and after meeting S. J. Davey, he would go on to co-develop the mal-observation paradigm to put their ideas to an empirical test.
</p><div class="figureView"><div class="short-legend"><p class="captionText"><span aria-level="3" role="heading"><span class="captionLabel">Figure 3. </span></span> A spirit portrait featuring Richard Hodgson. Taken with the purpose of demonstrating how to create fraudulent spirit photographs.<span class="ref-lnk lazy-ref en"><a data-rid="en0045" href="#" data-behaviour="toggle-ref" data-ref-type="fn" data-label="footnote"><span class="off-screen">Footnote</span><sup>45</sup></a></span>.</p></div><a href="#" class="thumbnail" data-behaviour="show-popup" data-popup-event-type="fig" data-id="f0003"><img id="d1e404" src="/cms/asset/ea50716c-9e68-4fc3-bbed-f7cd9478f0e5/ranr_a_2579758_f0003_oc.jpg" loading="lazy" height="500" width="354" alt="Figure 3. A spirit portrait featuring Richard Hodgson. Taken with the purpose of demonstrating how to create fraudulent spirit photographs.Footnote45."></a><div><button class="show-full-size btn btn-sm" data-behaviour="show-popup" data-id="f0003" data-popup-event-type="fig">Display full size</button></div></div><p></p><p>Hodgson’s co-experimenter, Samuel John Davey (<button class="ref show-table-fig-ref" data-id="f0004" data-behaviour="show-popup" data-popup-event-type="fig">Figure 4</button>), was an amateur magician. Before he began practising magic, Davey had been a true believer in the reality of spiritualist phenomena. He wrote that he initially came to his beliefs after seeing a recently deceased friend in a dream, and that his beliefs were further inspired by reading an English translation of Zöllner’s <i>Transcendental Physics</i>.<span class="ref-lnk lazy-ref en"><a data-rid="en0050" href="#" data-behaviour="toggle-ref" data-ref-type="fn" data-label="footnote"><span class="off-screen">Footnote</span><sup>50</sup></a></span> He also personally witnessed the apparently miraculous talents of the medium William Eglinton. Davey was particularly fascinated by the phenomenon of slate-writing.
